claims.text: The starting NbMoTaW alloy is equal-atomic and single-phase BCC.
Untreated NbMoTaW has excellent high-temperature strength up to approximately 1600 °C.
Untreated NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation resistance of untreated NbMoTaW has only been inferred computationally.
Adding Cr and V at a total concentration on the order of 5 at.% will improve the room-temperature ductility of NbMoTaW.
Adding Cr and V will improve the experimental irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW.
A W-Ta-V-Cr refractory high-entropy alloy can retain a single-phase BCC structure.
A W-Ta-V-Cr alloy exhibited no irradiation-created dislocation loops after irradiation to 8 dpa.
Cr/V-alloyed NbMoTaW will retain an overall single-phase BCC structure at high temperatures.
Cr and V additions will slightly increase lattice distortion in the NbMoTaW BCC matrix.
Cr and V additions may produce nanoscale segregation or a second-phase dispersion in NbMoTaW.
Cr and V additions will further equalize vacancy and interstitial mobilities.
Equalizing vacancy and interstitial mobilities will enhance defect recombination and irradiation tolerance.
Increased lattice distortion will enhance dislocation motion or activate additional slip systems at room temperature.
Enhanced dislocation motion or slip-system activation will improve room-temperature ductility without sacrificing high-temperature strength.
Cr/V-alloyed NbMoTaW will have lower irradiation-induced defect clustering than untreated NbMoTaW.
Cr/V-alloyed NbMoTaW will retain mechanical performance comparable to untreated NbMoTaW up to 1600 °C.
The proposed benefits will persist from room temperature to 1600 °C and under irradiation up to a few dpa.
Excessive Cr and V additions could induce multiphase formation or detrimental high-temperature precipitation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis seeks preservation of a single-phase BCC alloy, while the proposed mediator allows a second-phase dispersion. A material containing a genuine second phase is not strictly single-phase, even if BCC remains the dominant matrix.
